stories.headline: COP31: India presses historical responsibility and climate finance
stories.summary: At COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, India has put historical — cumulative — responsibility back at the centre of the negotiations, arguing that countries which emitted the most over time must lead both mitigation and finance efforts. Along with other developing countries, New Delhi contested the European Union's framing of climate finance, insisting that existing obligations under the UNFCCC and the Paris Agreement be honoured before new burdens are shifted to the Global South. India separately proposed a two-tier, country-driven Just Transition Mechanism and pressed for equity and climate justice in the outcome texts. Parallel discussions spotlighted the fragility of high mountain ranges after a proposed agenda item on the impacts of rising temperatures there was not taken up. Indian think-tank work on domestic resource mobilisation for climate action, and civil-society plantation drives tied to the UN Decade for Afforestation and Reforestation, ran alongside the formal talks.
stories.whyItMatters: COP31 outcomes will shape the climate finance architecture, the operationalisation of CBDR-RC and just transition support — all of which determine India's mitigation costs, energy transition pathway and standing as a voice of the Global South.

perspectives.take: Frames India as re-centring historical responsibility in the negotiating text and, in a parallel report, backing a two-tier, country-driven Just Transition Mechanism; Global South-oriented climate journalism.

static.topic: UNFCCC, Paris Agreement and India's climate commitments
static.syllabusNode: Environment — Climate Change
static.whatIsIt: The UNFCCC (1992) is the parent treaty; the Kyoto Protocol (1997) and the Paris Agreement (2015) operationalise it. India targets net-zero by 2070 and 50% installed non-fossil capacity by 2030.
static.background: Common But Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC) is the core equity principle of the regime. The Paris Agreement works through Nationally Determined Contributions and a ratchet mechanism. The Loss and Damage fund was operationalised at COP28 (2023). India leads the International Solar Alliance (2015) and the LiFE mission.
static.geography: Global regime; India's Himalayan, coastal and semi-arid regions are key climate-exposure zones.
static.socioEconomic: Climate finance gaps and transition costs bear on energy access, employment in coal-dependent districts and fiscal space.
static.whyInNews: At COP31 in Antalya, India invoked historical responsibility and demanded delivery on climate finance obligations.
static.wayForward: Deliver on finance and technology transfer, operationalise just transition support, and align NDC ambition with domestic resource mobilisation.
prelimsPointers: India's updated NDC: cut emissions intensity of GDP by 45% from 2005 levels by 2030.
Paris Agreement goal: keep warming well below 2°C, ideally 1.5°C.
static.mainsAngle: Examine the climate finance and technology transfer gaps, and assess equity in the Global Stocktake and just transition.

static.topic: UN-led multilateral negotiations and global governance
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs; the Security Council has five permanent veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members. The UNFCCC COP is the UN's universal climate negotiating forum.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and one of the largest troop contributors to peacekeeping. The G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) campaigns for UNSC expansion, and the Intergovernmental Negotiations on Security Council reform remain inconclusive.
static.socioEconomic: Multilateral outcomes on finance and technology shape developing countries' fiscal and industrial policy space.
static.whyInNews: COP31 in Antalya saw India and other developing countries contest EU positions on climate finance.
static.wayForward: Strengthen the representativeness and delivery credibility of multilateral institutions, linking climate governance reform to wider UN reform debates.
prelimsPointers: UNSC has 15 members: 5 permanent + 10 elected for two-year terms.
ICJ is in The Hague; UN headquarters is in New York.
static.mainsAngle: India's claim to a larger multilateral role rests on representativeness, population and contributions; assess the obstacles such as veto politics and the Ezulwini Consensus.

stories.headline: Trump, Xi, Putin meet; China and Russia issue joint 'peace declaration'
stories.summary: A trilateral meeting involving US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin took place on the sidelines of Trump's Asia tour, after which China and Russia jointly released a document described as a 'peace declaration'. The declaration, reported by wire services, is being read as a signal of Sino-Russian coordination at a moment when Washington is simultaneously engaging both capitals. The meeting came during a broader diplomatic swing through Asia by the US President, which also produced widely covered symbolic moments. Analysts have begun framing the three-way interaction as evidence of a shifting 'geometry' of global power rather than a settled institutional arrangement. The episode feeds directly into debates on multipolarity, ad hoc summitry and the space left for middle powers such as India.
stories.whyItMatters: Great-power summitry outside established institutions tests the rule-based multilateral order and directly conditions India's room for strategic autonomy and multi-alignment. UPSC repeatedly examines shifts in the global power balance, Sino-Russian alignment and India's balancing diplomacy.

perspectives.take: Straight wire report: the news peg is the China–Russia 'peace declaration' issued after the three leaders met, framed factually without interpretive spin.
Indian strategic-analysis framing: reads the Trump–Xi–Putin trilateral as a new geometry of global power, with implications for middle powers and India's positioning.

static.topic: India's Foreign Policy & Strategic Autonomy
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India & the World
static.whatIsIt: India's foreign policy combines strategic autonomy, multi-alignment, and the Neighbourhood First and Act East outlooks. It engages across the Quad, BRICS, SCO, G20 and IBSA simultaneously.
static.background: Rooted in NAM (1961) and Panchsheel (1954). Post-1991 liberalisation and the 1998 nuclear tests reshaped ties with the US. The Indo-Pacific concept and Quad (with US, Japan, Australia) gained salience after 2017.
static.whyInNews: A US–China–Russia trilateral and a China–Russia 'peace declaration' compress the strategic space in which India practises multi-alignment, raising the cost of balancing each relationship separately.
static.wayForward: Sustain issue-based engagement with all three powers, deepen Quad and Indo-Pacific partnerships without converting them into an alliance, and continue to act as a bridging voice for the Global South in BRICS, SCO and the G20.

static.topic: Great-Power Trilateralism and the Multilateral Order
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Groupings, Multilateral Fora & UN Reform
static.whatIsIt: Ad hoc summitry among the major powers — as opposed to treaty-based or charter-based institutions — has re-emerged as a mode of managing global order, alongside the UN system, G20, BRICS and SCO.
static.background: The post-1945 order vested primary peace-and-security responsibility in the UN Security Council, whose five permanent members hold veto power. Post-Cold War unipolarity gave way to a more contested distribution of power, prompting recurring proposals for UNSC reform, including the G4 demand (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan), discussed in the Intergovernmental Negotiations process.
static.whyInNews: The Trump–Xi–Putin meeting and the subsequent China–Russia 'peace declaration' illustrate decision-making shifting towards leader-level diplomacy outside formal multilateral channels.
static.wayForward: Push for inclusive institutional reform so that outcomes affecting the wider international community are not settled by a handful of powers; anchor positions in UN Charter principles of sovereignty and non-aggression.

The G4 — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — jointly advocates expansion of the permanent membership of the UNSC.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how ad hoc great-power summitry affects the legitimacy and effectiveness of charter-based multilateral institutions, and what it implies for India.

stories.headline: J&K forces kill Lateef Bhatt; Army officer rescues girls in Kulgam
stories.summary: In a reported counter-terror operation in Kulgam, Jammu and Kashmir, security forces killed Lateef Bhatt, described as a Lashkar commander, after tracking him through a dropped phone and CCTV trail. During the operation, an Army officer rescued 25 girls and two teachers while under heavy fire, according to Telegraph India. ThePrint detailed the surveillance trail, while The Hindu’s editorial argued that restoration of Statehood is essential for lasting peace in Jammu and Kashmir. The episode highlights both the tactical capabilities of Indian security forces and the unresolved political dimension of the Kashmir conflict.

static.topic: Jammu and Kashmir Statehood and Centre–State Relations
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Federalism & Devolution
static.whatIsIt: The demand to restore full Statehood to Jammu and Kashmir, which was reorganised into Union Territories in 2019, raising questions about federalism, representation and the constitutional status of the region.
static.background: India is a quasi-federal union with powers divided by the Seventh Schedule; residuary powers rest with the Union under Article 248. The Sarkaria (1983) and Punchhi (2007) Commissions reviewed Centre–State relations. The Governor (Article 153) is the Centre’s constitutional representative and has been a flashpoint over assent to Bills (Article 200) and reservation of Bills for the President (Article 201).
static.geography: Jammu and Kashmir, a Himalayan region with strategic borders; Kulgam district is in south Kashmir.
static.socioEconomic: Conflict-affected economy, high dependence on central transfers, tourism and horticulture; security disruptions affect livelihoods and education.
static.whyInNews: A counter-terror operation in Kulgam and The Hindu editorial’s argument that restoration of Statehood is essential for peace have renewed focus on J&K’s constitutional status.
static.wayForward: A calibrated political process, restoration of democratic institutions as appropriate, and cooperative federalism can complement security operations; any change must follow constitutional and legal procedures.

Inter-State Council (Art. 263) is a recommendatory dispute-resolution body.

static.wayForward: Sustain intelligence-led, human-rights-compliant operations; invest in local policing, deradicalisation, development and political outreach to prevent recruitment and reduce civilian harm.

stories.headline: Supreme Court weighs penalties for Yamuna pollution, invokes continuing mandamus
stories.summary: The Supreme Court is weighing the question of penalties for continuing pollution of the Yamuna, taking up the matter as part of its long-running supervision of river-cleaning efforts. Reports indicate the bench is examining liability for defaulting authorities rather than confining itself to fresh directions on sewage and effluent treatment. The issue surfaced alongside a wider batch of environment-related judicial orders, underscoring how routinely the court now drives environmental compliance. The underlying dispute concerns the heavily polluted Delhi stretch of the river, where untreated sewage and industrial discharge have persisted despite repeated orders. The court's approach reflects its established practice of keeping compliance under continuing review and using its power to pass any order necessary for complete justice.
stories.whyItMatters: It illustrates the judiciary's use of Article 32 and Article 142 — including continuing mandamus and penalty powers — to enforce environmental compliance where executive machinery has lagged. Useful for questions on judicial review, environmental governance and river conservation.

perspectives.take: Legal-reporting lens: frames the story around the bench's observations and the penalty/liability question, rather than the pollution data itself.
Environment-policy lens: places the order within a digest of major environment orders, stressing governance and compliance gaps over courtroom procedure.

static.topic: Supreme Court, High Courts and Judicial Review
static.syllabusNode: Polity and Governance — Judiciary: judicial review, writ jurisdiction, Article 142
static.whatIsIt: The Supreme Court (Art. 124) is the apex court and guardian of the Constitution; High Courts (Art. 214) sit at the state level. Judicial review is the power to test legislative and executive action against the Constitution.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine; PILs expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Articles 32 and 226 provide writ jurisdiction, and Article 142 allows the SC to pass any order needed for complete justice — the basis of 'continuing mandamus' in environmental litigation.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court is weighing penalties for continuing pollution of the Yamuna, exercising its monitoring jurisdiction over a long-running environmental matter.
static.wayForward: Strengthen specialised green benches and enforcement machinery so compliance does not depend on repeated judicial prodding; address judicial vacancies and pendency.

static.topic: Yamuna pollution and river rejuvenation
static.syllabusNode: Environment and Ecology — Pollution, river conservation, environmental governance
static.whatIsIt: The Yamuna is the longest tributary of the Ganga, rising at Yamunotri in Uttarakhand and joining the Ganga at Prayagraj. Its stretch through Delhi is the most polluted, dominated by untreated sewage and industrial effluent, and is the focus of long-standing judicial and administrative action.
static.background: Judicial attention to river pollution dates to the Ganga pollution litigation of the late 1980s (M.C. Mehta v. Union of India), which produced the 'continuing mandamus' technique. The polluter-pays and precautionary principles were articulated by the Supreme Court in the Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum case (1996). The Namami Gange Programme (2014) covers the Ganga and its tributaries, including the Yamuna; the National Green Tribunal (NGT Act, 2010) hears environmental disputes.
static.geography: Rises at Yamunotri (Uttarakhand); flows through Haryana, Delhi and Uttar Pradesh; joins the Ganga at Prayagraj (Triveni Sangam).
static.socioEconomic: The river supports irrigation, drinking water and livelihoods across several states; pollution imposes public-health costs and affects agriculture and tourism.
static.whyInNews: The Supreme Court is considering penalties for continuing Yamuna pollution, alongside a batch of environment-related orders.
static.wayForward: Interstate coordination on sewage treatment capacity, real-time water-quality monitoring, enforcement against industrial discharge, and riverfront and floodplain restoration.
prelimsPointers: Yamuna is the longest tributary of the Ganga; it joins the Ganga at Prayagraj.
Namami Gange Programme was launched in 2014 for the Ganga and its tributaries.
NGT was established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss why river-cleaning programmes underperform and whether judicial penalties can drive institutional accountability.

stories.headline: Bombay High Court quashes ICICI Bank's sanction to prosecute Chanda Kochhar
stories.summary: The Bombay High Court has set aside the sanction granted by ICICI Bank to prosecute its former chief, Chanda Kochhar, in the ICICI-Videocon loan case. The order removes the procedural foundation on which the prosecution against her was proceeding, and is being read as a setback for the investigating agencies. The underlying case relates to loans extended by ICICI Bank to the Videocon Group and allegations of conflict of interest and quid pro quo, which have been under investigation for several years. Legal commentators note that the ruling turns on the validity of the sanctioning decision rather than on the merits of the allegations themselves, leaving open the possibility of a fresh, validly granted sanction or of an appeal.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the procedural safeguards — sanction and prior approval — that stand between investigating agencies and the prosecution of senior banking and corporate figures. For UPSC, it links judicial review of administrative/statutory sanctions with banking-sector accountability and the interpretation of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

perspectives.take: A legal-reporting framing that foregrounds the High Court's act of setting aside the sanction, treating it as a procedural development in the ICICI-Videocon matter rather than a verdict on the allegations.
Highlights the identity of the sanctioning authority — that it was the bank (ICICI Bank) which granted the sanction — signalling that the legality of who sanctions and how is central to the dispute.

static.topic: High Courts, Judicial Review and Writ Jurisdiction
static.syllabusNode: Polity — Judiciary: Supreme Court, High Courts and judicial review
static.whatIsIt: High Courts are constitutional courts established under Article 214, with writ jurisdiction under Article 226 that is wider than the Supreme Court's under Article 32 because it extends to legal rights as well as fundamental rights. Judicial review is the power of courts to test executive and statutory action against the Constitution and the law.
static.background: The collegium system evolved through the Three Judges Cases (1981, 1993, 1998). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the basic-structure doctrine. Public Interest Litigation expanded access to justice from the late 1970s. Articles 32 and 226 are the writ jurisdictions of the Supreme Court and the High Courts respectively.
static.socioEconomic: High Courts are the principal forum for challenges to statutory sanctions, administrative orders and regulatory action, making their docket central to economic governance.
static.whyInNews: The Bombay High Court exercised its constitutional jurisdiction to set aside the sanction granted by ICICI Bank to prosecute Chanda Kochhar in the ICICI-Videocon loan case.
static.wayForward: Strengthen the capacity and reduce pendency of High Courts — through filling judicial vacancies, case-management reforms and specialised commercial/economic offences benches — so that high-stakes economic disputes are resolved without prolonged uncertainty.
prelimsPointers: High Courts are established under Article 214; their writ power under Article 226 is wider than Article 32 as it covers legal rights too.
Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Courts) are constitutional remedies; Article 226 is not itself a fundamental right.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how High Courts' writ jurisdiction balances executive/agency action against individual liberty and procedural fairness, using sanction-related litigation in economic offences as an illustration.

static.topic: Sanction and Prior Approval for Prosecution under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Statutory safeguards, accountability of public servants and anti-corruption framework
static.whatIsIt: The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 creates offences for public servants and provides procedural safeguards: Section 19 requires prior sanction of the competent authority before a court can take cognizance of an offence, and Section 17A (inserted by the 2018 amendment) requires prior approval before an inquiry, inquiry or investigation is conducted. Section 2(c) defines 'public servant'.
static.background: The PC Act, 1988 consolidated anti-corruption law, replacing the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The 2018 amendment inserted Section 17A and redefined certain provisions, tightening the process for investigating public servants. How these sanction and approval requirements apply to officials of private-sector banks has been a subject of legal debate, given the regulatory framework of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and the Reserve Bank of India's supervisory role.
static.socioEconomic: Sanction requirements are meant to prevent vexatious prosecution and shield honest decision-making, but critics argue they can delay or defeat genuine cases involving senior bank and corporate officials — a live concern for regulatory credibility and depositor confidence.
static.whyInNews: The Bombay High Court set aside the sanction granted by ICICI Bank to prosecute Chanda Kochhar, placing the validity of the sanctioning process at the centre of the ICICI-Videocon loan case.
static.wayForward: Clarify through legislation or authoritative judicial interpretation who the competent sanctioning authority is for different categories of bank officials, and prescribe time limits for sanction decisions so that safeguards do not become instruments of indefinite delay.
prelimsPointers: Section 19 of the PC Act makes prior sanction a condition precedent for a court to take cognizance of an offence under the Act.
Section 17A, inserted by the 2018 amendment to the PC Act, requires prior approval before initiating inquiry or investigation against a public servant.
The PC Act, 1988 replaced the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss whether procedural safeguards such as sanction and prior approval under the PC Act strengthen the integrity of investigations or insulate powerful officials from accountability, in the context of economic offences involving banks.

High Courts exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226, which extends to legal rights as well as fundamental rights — wider than the Supreme Court's power under Article 32.
stories.mainsQuestion: The requirement of sanction for prosecution is designed to protect honest public decision-making, but it can also delay or derail cases against powerful officials. Critically examine this tension in the context of economic offences involving banks, and suggest reforms to make the sanctioning process both fair and time-bound.

stories.headline: ICJ finds Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against Rohingya
stories.summary: The International Court of Justice has reportedly found Myanmar responsible for state-sponsored genocide against its Rohingya minority, according to Reuters — the first time the World Court has held a state accountable for genocide on the merits. The case was brought by The Gambia in November 2019 under Article IX of the 1948 Genocide Convention, arguing that all states parties share an interest in preventing genocide. The court had earlier ordered provisional measures in January 2020 requiring Myanmar to prevent genocidal acts and preserve evidence, and it rejected Myanmar's preliminary objections to jurisdiction in 2022, clearing the way for a merits ruling. The judgment carries enormous moral and legal weight but no automatic enforcement machinery, since compliance ultimately rests with the UN Security Council, where veto politics apply. It also sharpens scrutiny of the 2017 military crackdown in Rakhine State that drove over 700,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh.
stories.whyItMatters: A landmark test of the Genocide Convention and of the UN's enforcement architecture — directly relevant to GS-II questions on international law, global governance, UNSC reform and the Responsibility to Protect. It also feeds India's policy debate on Rohingya refugees, deportation and the absence of a domestic refugee law.

perspectives.take: The wire service leads with the legal first — a top UN court attributing state-sponsored genocide to Myanmar — framing it as a landmark accountability moment while implicitly flagging that enforcement now depends on the Security Council; a factual, outcome-focused Anglo-American wire framing with no stake in the verdict's politics.

static.topic: International Court of Justice and the Genocide Convention
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — International Institutions, International Law and Accountability
static.whatIsIt: The ICJ is the principal judicial organ of the United Nations, seated at the Peace Palace in The Hague. It settles disputes between states and gives advisory opinions to UN organs. The 1948 Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide declares genocide a crime under international law and, under Article IX, allows disputes between state parties over its interpretation or application to be taken to the ICJ.
static.background: The Genocide Convention was adopted in 1948 in the shadow of the Holocaust and entered into force in 1951; India ratified it in 1959. The Gambia filed an application against Myanmar before the ICJ in November 2019 alleging violations of the Convention against the Rohingya. The court ordered provisional measures in January 2020 directing Myanmar to prevent genocidal acts, preserve evidence and report periodically. In July 2022 the ICJ rejected Myanmar's preliminary objections, upholding jurisdiction and allowing the case to move to the merits.
static.geography: The Hague, Netherlands (seat of the ICJ); Rakhine State, Myanmar; The Gambia as applicant state; Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar district hosting the bulk of the refugee outflow.
static.socioEconomic: The Rohingya, a largely Muslim minority in Rakhine State, were rendered effectively stateless by Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law, with restrictions on movement, education, livelihoods and marriage. Over 700,000 fled to Bangladesh after the August 2017 military crackdown, creating one of the world's largest protracted refugee situations and a heavy humanitarian and security burden on the region.
static.whyInNews: Reuters reports that the ICJ has found Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against the Rohingya — the first merits finding of state responsibility for genocide in the court's history.
static.wayForward: Because the ICJ has no enforcement police, compliance rests on Article 94 of the UN Charter, which allows the Security Council to give effect to judgments — a route blocked by P5 veto politics. Parallel accountability is being pursued through the International Criminal Court and domestic universal-jurisdiction proceedings, while the focus shifts to reparations, refugee return conditions and safeguards for the remaining Rohingya in Rakhine State.
prelimsPointers: ICJ has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms; it hears disputes between states, not individuals, and sits at The Hague.
ICJ judgments bind only the parties to the case and are not self-enforcing; enforcement may be referred to the UN Security Council under Article 94 of the UN Charter.
India ratified the Genocide Convention in 1959 and is a party to it.
static.mainsAngle: The ICJ's genocide finding against Myanmar tests the enforcement architecture of international law. Examine the limits of judicial accountability when enforcement depends on a veto-bound Security Council, and suggest reforms.

static.topic: United Nations and Multilateral Reform
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Global Governance and UN Reform
static.whatIsIt: The UN (1945) has six principal organs. The Security Council has 15 members — five permanent, veto-wielding members (P5) and ten elected members serving two-year terms. India has long sought permanent UNSC membership, arguing that the body's composition no longer reflects contemporary geopolitics.
static.background: India is a founding UN member and among the largest troop contributors to UN peacekeeping. The G4 — India, Brazil, Germany and Japan — campaigns for UNSC expansion, while the African group's Ezulwini Consensus demands at least two permanent seats with veto rights for Africa. The Intergovernmental Negotiations (IGN) process on Security Council reform has remained inconclusive for years.
static.whyInNews: A landmark ICJ verdict against a state has spotlighted the gap between legal findings and Security Council enforcement, reviving debate on UNSC reform, veto restraint and the operational reach of the Responsibility to Protect.
static.wayForward: Move the IGN towards text-based negotiations, engage the African bloc on a common expansion formula, and build support for voluntary veto restraint in mass-atrocity situations as a stepping stone to structural reform.
prelimsPointers: UNSC: 5 permanent + 10 elected members (two-year terms); the veto applies only to substantive, not procedural, matters.
ICJ is at The Hague; UN headquarters is in New York.
Article 94 of the UN Charter empowers the Security Council to enforce ICJ judgments.
static.mainsAngle: Does the UN's Security Council-dependent enforcement architecture render ICJ genocide findings hollow? Critically examine in the light of the Myanmar verdict.

static.topic: Rohingya Crisis and India's Response
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and Neighbourhood; Refugee Policy
static.whatIsIt: The Rohingya are a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority in Myanmar's Rakhine State who were effectively stripped of citizenship by the 1982 Citizenship Law. India, which is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention or its 1967 Protocol and has no domestic refugee law, deals with Rohingya arrivals under the Foreigners Act and discretionary administrative practice.
static.background: Large-scale Rohingya displacement followed successive waves of persecution, most acutely after the August 2017 military operations in Rakhine State, when over 700,000 fled to Bangladesh. India has raised the issue bilaterally with Myanmar and has linked long-term return to Myanmar's own verification processes.
static.geography: Rakhine State (Myanmar), Cox's Bazar (Bangladesh) and scattered Rohingya settlements in India including Jammu, Hyderabad and Delhi-NCR.
static.socioEconomic: Refugee hosting strains local infrastructure and livelihoods, and Rohingya populations in India face documentation barriers, detention risk and limited access to education and formal work.
static.whyInNews: The ICJ's genocide finding renews pressure on host states, including India, to clarify the legal status of Rohingya refugees and to reassess deportation decisions in the light of the court's conclusions.
static.wayForward: Enacting a domestic refugee law consistent with non-refoulement, strengthening regional coordination with Bangladesh and ASEAN on safe, voluntary and dignified returns, and pressing Myanmar on citizenship and rights restoration.
prelimsPointers: India is not a signatory to the 1951 Refugee Convention or the 1967 Protocol and has no dedicated refugee legislation.
Myanmar's 1982 Citizenship Law excluded the Rohingya from the list of recognised national races, rendering them effectively stateless.
The ICJ adjudicates state responsibility; the ICC tries individuals for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.
static.mainsAngle: In the light of the ICJ's genocide finding, examine whether India's executive-driven refugee policy is adequate to meet its international law obligations towards the Rohingya.

prelims: ICJ (The Hague) is the principal judicial organ of the UN; it settles inter-state disputes and gives advisory opinions, and its judgments are binding but not self-enforcing.
The 1948 Genocide Convention makes genocide a crime under international law and, under Article IX, allows disputes between state parties to be referred to the ICJ; India ratified it in 1959.
Enforcement of ICJ judgments rests with the UN Security Council under Article 94 of the UN Charter, where any P5 veto can block action.
ICJ versus ICC: the ICJ tries states; the ICC (Rome Statute) tries individuals for genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression.
stories.mainsQuestion: The International Court of Justice's genocide finding against Myanmar is a milestone in international law, yet its enforcement depends on a veto-bound Security Council. Critically examine the implications for the Genocide Convention, the Responsibility to Protect and India's own refugee policy.

stories.headline: Board of Peace faults Israel and Hamas as Gaza plan stalls
stories.summary: The Board of Peace associated with US President Donald Trump's Gaza plan has publicly held both Israel and Hamas responsible for the failure to move beyond the ceasefire to a full settlement. While the truce has stopped large-scale fighting, the broader framework — under which Hamas is to disarm, Israeli troops are to withdraw and reconstruction is to begin — has been effectively frozen since shortly after it took effect last year. The criticism from the body signals growing frustration that neither party has met its sequenced obligations. The impasse leaves Gaza's humanitarian and reconstruction needs unaddressed and keeps the wider political question of Palestinian statehood unresolved.
stories.whyItMatters: The Gaza impasse is a live test case for ceasefire design, post-conflict reconstruction and the credibility of externally brokered peace frameworks in West Asia — all recurring themes in GS-II International Relations. It also directly bears on India's balancing act between its strategic partnership with Israel, its traditional support for Palestinian statehood and its Gulf interests.

perspectives.take: International desk report framing the story as a mutual failure of Israel and Hamas to convert a working ceasefire into the wider plan; neutral, wire-style coverage that avoids assigning primary blame to either side.

The same report carried on the paper's main feed, with identical framing — the emphasis falls on the stalled elements (disarmament, withdrawal, reconstruction) rather than on apportioning responsibility.

static.topic: West Asia Peace Process and the Two-State Solution
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements involving India and/or affecting India's interests; effect of policies of developed countries on India's interests
static.whatIsIt: The decades-long diplomatic effort to resolve the Israeli–Palestinian conflict around the two-state formula: an independent Palestinian state existing alongside Israel, broadly on the pre-1967 lines with agreed land swaps, a shared arrangement for Jerusalem and a just settlement of the refugee question.
static.background: The dispute traces back to the 1947 UN partition plan and the 1948–49 war. UNSC Resolution 242 (1967) and Resolution 338 (1973) established the 'land for peace' framework. The Oslo Accords (1993) created the Palestinian Authority and a phased self-rule process, dividing the West Bank into Areas A, B and C; subsequent rounds at Camp David (2000) and Annapolis (2007) failed. The Abraham Accords (2020) normalised Israel's relations with several Arab states while leaving the Palestinian question unresolved. The Gaza war that began in October 2023, the ceasefire that followed and the multi-phase plan now under discussion have revived debate on disarmament, Israeli withdrawal and reconstruction.
static.geography: Levant / eastern Mediterranean. The Gaza Strip is a narrow coastal territory bordering Israel and Egypt (Rafah crossing) on the Mediterranean.
static.socioEconomic: Gaza's economy and civilian infrastructure have been devastated; humanitarian access, aid dependence, unemployment and the financing of reconstruction are central to any settlement.
static.whyInNews: The Board of Peace tied to the US President's Gaza plan has faulted both Israel and Hamas for the stalled implementation of the wider plan — Hamas disarmament, Israeli troop withdrawal and reconstruction — even though the ceasefire has halted major fighting.
static.wayForward: Sequenced implementation with credible third-party monitoring, guaranteed humanitarian access, a politically legitimate Palestinian authority, regional guarantors (Egypt, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye) and a defined pathway back to a negotiated two-state settlement.
prelimsPointers: UNSC Resolution 242 (1967) enunciated the 'land for peace' principle; Resolution 338 (1973) called for its implementation.
The Oslo Accords (1993) created the Palestinian Authority and divided the West Bank into Areas A, B and C.
static.mainsAngle: Evaluate the viability of the two-state solution in the light of shifting regional alignments and stalled post-conflict arrangements in Gaza.

static.topic: India–Israel and India–Palestine Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and the World; bilateral, regional and global groupings and agreements affecting India's interests
static.whatIsIt: India's parallel engagement with Israel (defence, agriculture, water, technology, trade) and with Palestine (political support, development assistance, capacity building), historically balanced through consistent backing for a two-state solution.
static.background: India recognised Israel in 1950 but established full diplomatic relations only in 1992. It has long supported the Palestinian cause at the United Nations, was among the first non-Arab states to recognise the Palestine Liberation Organization, and maintains a representative office in Ramallah. The 'de-hyphenation' of the two relationships became visible from the mid-2010s, with standalone prime ministerial visits to Israel (2017) and to Palestine. India has sent humanitarian assistance to Gaza during successive escalations.
static.socioEconomic: India's stakes include energy security and the safety of a large diaspora in the Gulf, alongside defence procurement and technology cooperation with Israel.
static.whyInNews: The stalled Gaza plan and the Board of Peace's criticism of both parties sharpen India's dilemma of balancing its strategic partnership with Israel against its traditional support for Palestinian statehood and its Gulf interests.
static.wayForward: Continue principled support for a two-state solution, humanitarian assistance and UN-centred diplomacy while safeguarding strategic, energy and diaspora interests.
prelimsPointers: India established full diplomatic relations with Israel in 1992.
India was among the first non-Arab states to recognise the Palestine Liberation Organization.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how India balances its strategic partnership with Israel and its historical support for Palestine in a changing West Asian order.

static.topic: International Humanitarian Law and Humanitarian Access in Armed Conflict
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — humanitarian issues and international institutions; GS-III — security and disaster relief
static.whatIsIt: The body of law — the Geneva Conventions and their Additional Protocols, together with customary international humanitarian law — governing conduct in armed conflict, the protection of civilians, prisoners and humanitarian personnel, and the obligation to permit relief operations.
static.background: The four Geneva Conventions (1949) and their Additional Protocols (1977) form the core of IHL. The UN Security Council has repeatedly affirmed the need for unhindered humanitarian access in conflict zones. UNRWA, established in 1949, is the principal relief agency for Palestinian refugees.
static.socioEconomic: Aid dependence, movement restrictions and the destruction of civilian infrastructure shape living conditions and reconstruction prospects in Gaza.
static.whyInNews: With the wider Gaza plan stalled, questions of humanitarian access, civilian protection and who finances and manages reconstruction remain unresolved.
static.wayForward: Strengthen compliance and accountability mechanisms, protect humanitarian personnel, and link relief operations to a durable political settlement rather than treating them as a substitute for one.
prelimsPointers: The Geneva Conventions of 1949 and their Additional Protocols of 1977 are the core instruments of international humanitarian law.
UNRWA was established in 1949 to assist Palestinian refugees.
static.mainsAngle: Examine the adequacy of international humanitarian law in protecting civilians in contemporary urban conflicts.

prelims: The Board of Peace associated with the US President's Gaza plan has faulted both Israel and Hamas for the failure to implement the wider plan.
The plan's core elements are Hamas disarmament, Israeli troop withdrawal and the start of reconstruction in Gaza.
A ceasefire halted major fighting, but the broader plan has been effectively stalled since soon after it came into effect last year.
stories.mainsQuestion: The Gaza ceasefire has halted major fighting, yet the wider political plan remains stalled. Analyse the obstacles to implementing disarmament, withdrawal and reconstruction, and assess the implications for India's West Asia policy.

stories.headline: Bangladesh deploys paramilitary units as unrest over Hasina's return spreads
stories.summary: Bangladesh has moved paramilitary forces into the streets as political unrest widens around the question of Sheikh Hasina's return to the country. According to The Hindu, citing local media, police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and cases of vehicles being torched across at least 28 districts over the past ten days, with police personnel and civilians among the injured. The friction reflects the unfinished polarisation left by the 2024 mass uprising that removed Hasina from power, and it complicates the interim administration's stated road map back to elected rule. For India, the turbulence sits directly on its longest land border and touches transit, trade, energy and minority-security interests, making Dhaka's stability a core neighbourhood concern.
stories.whyItMatters: Bangladesh is central to India's Neighbourhood First policy — unrest there directly implicates border management, connectivity, trade and internal security. The story also feeds GS-II questions on political instability in South Asia and its spillover into India's interests.

perspectives.take: Coverage available at source.

static.topic: India–Bangladesh Relations
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — India and its Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: The bilateral relationship between India and Bangladesh, spanning a land border of about 4,096 km — the longest India shares with any neighbour — along with trade, water-sharing, connectivity, energy and security cooperation.
static.background: Bangladesh was born in 1971 with Indian political and military support, and ties were formalised through the 1972 India–Bangladesh Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Peace. Cooperation deepened via the 1996 Ganga Waters Treaty, the 2015 Land Boundary Agreement that exchanged enclaves, and agreements on transit, port access and power trade. Relations entered a period of uncertainty after the August 2024 political transition in Dhaka, with the ousted Awami League's future and minority security emerging as live issues.
static.geography: Bangladesh borders West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; India and Bangladesh share 54 common rivers and the Ganga–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta, with the Bay of Bengal anchoring maritime and port-based connectivity.
static.socioEconomic: Bangladesh is one of India's largest export destinations in South Asia and benefits from duty-free access as a least developed country; connectivity projects such as access to Chattogram and Mongla ports, rail links and cross-border power trade carry significant economic value, while migration and minority welfare remain politically sensitive.
static.whyInNews: Escalating unrest in Bangladesh, including crude bomb blasts and vehicle arson across at least 28 districts and the deployment of paramilitary forces, has revived concern in India about stability across its eastern border.
static.wayForward: Institutionalise water-sharing negotiations ahead of the 2026 renewal cycle of the Ganga treaty, insulate transit, trade and power links from political swings, and pursue sustained people-to-people and minority-protection diplomacy.
prelimsPointers: India–Bangladesh land border is about 4,096 km, the longest India shares with any neighbour.
The Ganga Waters Treaty was signed in 1996 for a 30-year term, so it comes up for renewal in 2026.
The 2015 Land Boundary Agreement operationalised the exchange of enclaves between India and Bangladesh.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how political instability in Bangladesh tests India's Neighbourhood First policy, and suggest measures to de-risk bilateral cooperation from regime change.

static.topic: BIMSTEC and Regional Cooperation in South Asia
static.syllabusNode: International Relations — Regional Groupings and India's Neighbourhood
static.whatIsIt: The Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation, a seven-member grouping that connects South Asia with Southeast Asia across connectivity, trade, energy and security sectors.
static.background: Established in 1997 through the Bangkok Declaration, the grouping expanded its membership and was renamed BIMSTEC in 2004; its permanent secretariat is located in Dhaka. It has gained prominence as regional cooperation through SAARC slowed, and India positions it as a bridge between its Act East and neighbourhood policies.
static.geography: The grouping is anchored in the Bay of Bengal littoral, drawing together the Himalayan states, the Indian subcontinent's eastern flank and mainland Southeast Asia.
static.socioEconomic: BIMSTEC's agenda covers a connectivity master plan, energy grid cooperation, trade facilitation and coastal shipping, all of which depend on political stability in member states such as Bangladesh.
static.whyInNews: Instability in Bangladesh — a founding member and host of BIMSTEC's secretariat — can stall the grouping's connectivity and trade agenda.
static.wayForward: Strengthen the secretariat's capacity, deliver early-harvest connectivity projects, and keep technical and economic cooperation functional even when bilateral politics in a member state turn adverse.
prelimsPointers: BIMSTEC has seven members: India, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand.
BIMSTEC's permanent secretariat is in Dhaka, while SAARC's secretariat is in Kathmandu.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether BIMSTEC can emerge as the primary vehicle for South Asian regionalism in the context of SAARC's decline and political volatility in member states.

static.topic: Paramilitary Forces and Internal Security Governance
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Role of Paramilitary and Armed Police Forces
static.whatIsIt: Paramilitary and armed police forces are deployed for border guarding, riot control, counter-insurgency and armed support to civil administration; in India they function under the Ministry of Home Affairs, and in Bangladesh under the home ministry framework.
static.background: India's Central Armed Police Forces grew out of the need to provide armed support to civil authority and to guard long and difficult borders. Bangladesh's border-guarding force is the Border Guard Bangladesh, earlier called the Bangladesh Rifles; the Rapid Action Battalion and district police handle internal law-and-order, with paramilitary units called in during major unrest.
static.whyInNews: Bangladesh has deployed paramilitary forces after police recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and incidents of vehicle burning across at least 28 districts in ten days.
static.wayForward: Ensure proportionality and accountability in the use of armed forces for internal order, maintain clear civil-authority control, and protect civilians and journalists during unrest.
prelimsPointers: India's Central Armed Police Forces include CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP, SSB and Assam Rifles.
Assam Rifles functions under the Ministry of Home Affairs but is operationally employed with the Indian Army.
Bangladesh's principal border-guarding force is the Border Guard Bangladesh, formerly the Bangladesh Rifles.
static.mainsAngle: Examine the role, legal framework and accountability of paramilitary forces in maintaining internal security in South Asian democracies.

prelims: Unrest in Bangladesh has been marked by dozens of crude bomb blasts and vehicle-arson incidents across at least 28 districts in ten days, with police personnel and civilians injured, according to local media reports cited by The Hindu.
Sheikh Hasina was removed from power in August 2024 following a student-led mass uprising, and her possible return has become a flashpoint in Bangladeshi politics.
Bangladesh is a founding member of BIMSTEC, whose permanent secretariat is located in Dhaka, and shares with India a border of about 4,096 km.
stories.mainsQuestion: Political volatility in India's neighbourhood frequently spills over into its security and economic interests. In this context, examine the implications of the unrest in Bangladesh for India's Neighbourhood First policy, and suggest measures to insulate bilateral cooperation from political change in Dhaka.

static.topic: UPI, MDR and the economics of digital payments
static.syllabusNode: Economy — Digital Payments and Financial Inclusion
static.whatIsIt: UPI is an interoperable, real-time retail payment system run by NPCI. MDR is the fee a merchant pays the acquiring bank or payment provider for accepting a payment; UPI person-to-merchant (P2M) transactions have been zero-MDR since 2020, with the government supporting small merchants through an incentive scheme.
static.background: UPI was launched by NPCI in 2016. From January 1, 2020, RBI/NPCI mandated zero charges on UPI and RuPay debit card transactions, and the government introduced a merchant-incentive scheme to compensate payment providers for low-value BHIM-UPI P2M and RuPay debit transactions. The model has driven volume growth but left providers dependent on timely subsidy flows. A separate MDR framework, including a reported flat ₹5 fee for B2B UPI, is under discussion.
static.socioEconomic: Zero-MDR has helped small merchants adopt digital payments, but unpaid incentives can squeeze fintechs and payment service providers; any B2B MDR must balance provider viability with merchant costs.
static.whyInNews: Fintechs report unpaid UPI incentives while the proposed MDR framework, including a likely flat ₹5 B2B UPI fee, faces delays.
static.wayForward: Publish a clear, time-bound MDR and incentive calendar; ring-fence and disburse verified dues; differentiate small-merchant P2M from B2B and large-merchant flows; assess price elasticity before levying fees.

MDR is paid by the merchant, not the customer, to the acquiring bank or payment provider.
UPI P2M transactions have carried zero MDR since January 2020, supported by government merchant incentives.
B2B UPI is a distinct segment from person-to-merchant UPI.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether zero-MDR is a sustainable long-term model for UPI and how a differentiated MDR regime can protect small merchants while ensuring payment providers recover costs.

static.topic: Digital Public Infrastructure: UPI and NPCI
static.syllabusNode: Governance — e-Governance and Data
static.whatIsIt: India's Digital Public Infrastructure is a layered, interoperable stack including Aadhaar, UPI and DigiLocker. UPI, operated by NPCI, is a real-time payment rail; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs personal data processing.
static.background: Aadhaar, run by UIDAI, was launched in 2009 and is the world's largest biometric ID system. UPI, launched by NPCI in 2016, processes billions of monthly transactions. The DPDP Act 2023 introduces a Data Protection Board and consent-based processing.
static.socioEconomic: UPI lowered transaction costs and expanded financial inclusion; the sustainability of the model depends on viable economics for private payment service providers.
static.whyInNews: Payment firms' unpaid incentives and the delayed MDR framework highlight the financing model behind UPI.
static.wayForward: Treat UPI as public infrastructure but design transparent, fiscally sustainable compensation for private payment service providers.
prelimsPointers: NPCI operates UPI, RuPay, IMPS and NACH.
The DPDP Act 2023 provides for consent, data-principal rights and significant data fiduciaries.
static.mainsAngle: Balance innovation with privacy and state surveillance; examine DPI as a global export model and its financing sustainability.

prelims: MDR is the merchant discount rate — a fee paid by the merchant to the acquiring bank or payment provider for accepting a digital payment.
UPI is operated by NPCI; person-to-merchant UPI transactions have been zero-MDR since January 2020, with government incentives for small merchants.
The reported proposal under discussion is a flat ₹5 MDR on B2B UPI transactions.
B2B UPI is distinct from P2M UPI; the two segments can have different pricing rules.
stories.mainsQuestion: Zero-MDR has been central to UPI's mass adoption, but it has left payment providers dependent on government incentives. Examine the case for a differentiated MDR framework for UPI, including B2B transactions, and suggest safeguards for small merchants.

stories.headline: Ayushman Bharat to expand government hospital packages from 23 to 112
stories.summary: The Tribune reports that the Ayushman Bharat scheme is set to widen the list of treatment packages available for procedures carried out in government hospitals, taking the count from 23 to 112. The change relates to the benefit packages offered under the scheme's health-insurance arm, PM-JAY, which was launched in 2018 and covers secondary and tertiary hospitalisation for eligible families. A longer package list for public facilities is presented as enabling government hospitals to offer a broader range of treatments under the scheme. The development sits within India's wider shift towards entitlement-based welfare delivered through DBT-backed, Aadhaar-linked systems.
stories.whyItMatters: Ayushman Bharat is a flagship welfare and social-security programme, so any change in its package architecture is directly relevant to GS-II questions on welfare design, health equity and delivery capacity. It also feeds the debate on whether insurance-based models can substitute for strengthening the public health system.

perspectives.take: Frames the story as a scheme-expansion measure, foregrounding the numerical jump in government-hospital packages (23 to 112) as the core news peg; a national daily with a broadly centrist, governance-focused framing.

articles.title: Ayushman Bharat scheme to expand government hospital packages from 23 to 112
articles.snippet: Ayushman Bharat scheme to expand government hospital packages from 23 to 112 The Tribune

static.topic: Ayushman Bharat and India's welfare architecture
static.syllabusNode: Social Justice — Welfare Schemes, Rights and Entitlements
static.whatIsIt: Ayushman Bharat, launched in 2018, is India's flagship health-welfare programme with two arms: the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana (PM-JAY), a health-insurance component, and the network of Health and Wellness Centres. It operates within a welfare model that combines rights-based legislation with DBT-enabled delivery over the JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) backbone.
static.background: India's welfare model blends rights-based laws — MGNREGA (2005), the Right to Education (2009) and the National Food Security Act (2013) — with Direct Benefit Transfer and the JAM trinity. Ayushman Bharat (2018) added a health-insurance arm (PM-JAY) and Health and Wellness Centres; POSHAN Abhiyaan addresses malnutrition. Article 15/16 and Indra Sawhney (1992) frame reservation policy, while the four labour codes consolidate 29 labour laws.
static.geography: Pan-India scheme; package utilisation and empanelment patterns differ sharply between high-focus and better-served States.
static.socioEconomic: Health shocks are a leading cause of household impoverishment in India; insurance-based cover is aimed at reducing catastrophic out-of-pocket spending, but awareness, empanelment and hospital capacity determine who actually benefits.
static.whyInNews: The Tribune reports that packages available for government hospitals under the scheme are to be expanded from 23 to 112, broadening the range of procedures public facilities can offer under PM-JAY.
static.wayForward: Pair package expansion with upgradation of public hospital capacity, staff and diagnostics; strengthen empanelment and grievance redressal; track denial rates and out-of-pocket spending to measure real financial protection rather than enrolment numbers.
prelimsPointers: Ayushman Bharat was launched in 2018 with two components: PM-JAY (health insurance) and Health and Wellness Centres.
PM-JAY covers secondary and tertiary hospitalisation, with benefit packages defining the procedures and rates payable.
PM-JAY is cited in the welfare-architecture card alongside MGNREGA, RTE and NFSA as part of India's entitlement-plus-DBT model.
static.mainsAngle: Examine how far insurance-based welfare schemes such as PM-JAY address exclusion errors and health-induced impoverishment compared with direct public provisioning of health services.

static.topic: Universal Health Coverage and public health financing
static.syllabusNode: Health — Government Policies and Interventions; Issues relating to development of health sector
static.whatIsIt: Universal Health Coverage means ensuring that all people receive needed health services without suffering financial hardship. In India it is pursued through a mix of publicly funded health infrastructure, government insurance schemes such as PM-JAY, and regulation of private provision.
static.background: India's public health spending has historically been low relative to comparable economies, with households bearing a large share of costs through out-of-pocket payments. The National Health Policy, 2017 set a direction of raising public health expenditure toward 2.5 per cent of GDP. Ayushman Bharat (2018) was introduced as a demand-side financing intervention alongside supply-side investments in Health and Wellness Centres.
static.geography: Inter-State variation in health infrastructure, doctor density and insurance empanelment shapes outcomes.
static.socioEconomic: Low public spending pushes households towards private care and borrowing; expanding public-facility packages aims to shift some of that demand back to government hospitals.
static.whyInNews: The reported expansion of PM-JAY packages for government hospitals is a demand-side intervention intended to make public facilities more usable under the scheme.
static.wayForward: Move beyond insurance expansion to sustained increases in public health expenditure, primary-care strengthening, health-human-resource gaps and regulation of private hospitals' pricing and denial practices.
keyTerms: Public health expenditure as share of GDP
prelimsPointers: The National Health Policy, 2017 indicated a target of raising public health expenditure to 2.5 per cent of GDP.
India's health financing relies substantially on out-of-pocket household spending, which insurance schemes seek to reduce.
Ayushman Bharat (2018) combines a demand-side insurance arm with supply-side Health and Wellness Centres.
static.mainsAngle: Assess whether demand-side insurance schemes can deliver universal health coverage in the absence of adequate public health infrastructure and spending.

prelims: Ayushman Bharat, launched in 2018, has two arms: PM-JAY (health insurance) and Health and Wellness Centres.
PM-JAY provides cover for secondary and tertiary hospitalisation, delivered through defined Health Benefit Packages.
As per The Tribune, the number of packages available for government hospitals under the scheme is being raised from 23 to 112.
The scheme sits within India's welfare architecture that combines rights-based laws with DBT and the JAM (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile) backbone.
stories.mainsQuestion: The widening of benefit packages under Ayushman Bharat is presented as an expansion of health coverage. Critically examine whether insurance-based demand-side financing, without commensurate growth in public health spending and public hospital capacity, can advance universal health coverage in India.

stories.headline: Amritpal Singh gets three-hour parole; Punjab under heavy security cover
stories.summary: Amritpal Singh, the pro-Khalistan preacher who heads Waris Punjab De and is a sitting Lok Sabha member, was allowed a three-hour parole to visit his home in Punjab, with the state government mounting a 72-hour security deployment around the visit. Police and paramilitary personnel were positioned along the route and at the family residence, and Punjab was placed on alert with restrictions on gatherings and movement near the site. The release was a short, conditional custody parole granted under escort and subject to conditions, not bail or acquittal. The episode has renewed debate on how a state balances a detainee's personal liberty against public order in a region with a history of militant mobilisation.
stories.whyItMatters: It is a live case study on preventive detention, parole administration and the internal security calculus in Punjab — themes that recur in GS-III internal security and GS-II governance/fundamental rights questions.

perspectives.take: Frames the event primarily through a security lens — the scale of the deployment, the 72-hour cover and the statewide alert — rather than through the legal basis or justification for granting parole to a high-profile detainee.

static.topic: National Security Act, 1980 (NSA)
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Preventive detention laws and their safeguards
static.whatIsIt: A preventive detention law that allows the Centre or a state to detain a person without trial for up to 12 months to prevent them from acting in a manner prejudicial to national security, public order, or the maintenance of essential supplies and services.
static.background: Promulgated as an ordinance in 1980 and enacted as the National Security Act, it replaced the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA), 1971, which had been widely misused during the Emergency. The Act was amended in 1987. Detention orders are typically executed by district magistrates or commissioners of police; the grounds of detention must be communicated to the detainee, who has a right to make a representation, and detention beyond three months requires the opinion of an Advisory Board.
static.socioEconomic: Critics argue preventive detention is disproportionately used against the poor, minorities and political opponents, and that the low rate of confirmation by Advisory Boards points to arbitrary use.
static.whyInNews: Amritpal Singh, who has been in detention under the NSA, was granted a short custody parole amid a large security deployment in Punjab.
static.wayForward: Strict adherence to procedural safeguards — timely communication of grounds, genuine access to representation, periodic judicial review — and consideration of a uniform national framework for temporary release of preventive detainees.
prelimsPointers: Under the NSA, a person may be detained for up to 12 months; detention beyond three months requires the opinion of an Advisory Board.

Article 22(4)–(7) of the Constitution permits preventive detention beyond three months only on the opinion of an Advisory Board, and provides safeguards such as communication of grounds and the right of representation.
The NSA, 1980 replaced the Maintenance of Internal Security Act, 1971.
static.mainsAngle: Examine whether preventive detention laws such as the NSA are compatible with the constitutional scheme of liberty, and suggest procedural and institutional safeguards to prevent misuse.

static.topic: Parole and furlough in India's prison system
static.syllabusNode: Governance — Criminal justice system and prison reform
static.whatIsIt: Parole is the conditional release of a prisoner or detainee before the end of the sentence, granted for a short period and usually for specific reasons such as a family emergency, medical treatment or court appearances. Furlough is a periodical release, generally for a longer duration, treated as a matter of right under state prison rules rather than a concession.
static.background: Prison administration is a State List subject under Entry 4 of List II, so parole and furlough rules vary across states and derive mainly from the Prisons Act, 1894 and state prison manuals. The Supreme Court has held that parole is a discretionary concession and not a right, while furlough under most state rules is treated as a right. The Model Prisons Act, 2023 was circulated to states to modernise and harmonise prison law, including provisions on the welfare of prisoners and temporary release.
static.socioEconomic: Prison overcrowding and inconsistent parole rules across states mean that access to temporary release often depends on the state where a person is lodged rather than on uniform standards.
static.whyInNews: The short parole granted in this case, with elaborate security conditions attached, illustrates how parole decisions for high-profile detainees are shaped by public order considerations.
static.wayForward: Adoption of the Model Prisons Act, 2023 by states, codified and transparent criteria for granting or refusing parole, and clear written conditions where security concerns warrant restrictions.
prelimsPointers: Parole is a discretionary, short-term conditional release; furlough is a periodical release generally treated as a right under state prison rules.
Prisons and prison administration fall under the State List, so parole and furlough rules differ from state to state.
The Prisons Act, 1894 remains the principal central legislation in the field; the Model Prisons Act, 2023 was circulated to states for adoption.
static.mainsAngle: Discuss how the discretionary nature of parole can be reconciled with the right to personal liberty, and assess the case for uniform national standards on temporary release.

static.topic: Radicalism and internal security in Punjab
static.syllabusNode: Internal Security — Extremism, radicalisation and cross-border dimensions
static.whatIsIt: Punjab witnessed a militant separatist movement from the late 1970s to the early 1990s demanding a separate Sikh state ('Khalistan'). In recent years, radical activity has revived in a different form — driven substantially by diaspora-based outfits, social media mobilisation and small, high-visibility confrontations with the state rather than by sustained armed insurgency.
static.background: The demand grew out of the Punjabi Suba movement that led to the reorganisation of Punjab in 1966 and the Anandpur Sahib Resolution of 1973. The 1980s saw escalating militancy, Operation Blue Star in June 1984, the anti-Sikh violence of 1984, and a period of insurgency that declined by the mid-1990s. The recent phase includes diaspora campaigns such as the Referendum 2020 initiative of Sikhs for Justice, the formation of the outfit Waris Punjab De in 2021, and a series of law-and-order episodes in Punjab in 2022–23.
static.geography: Punjab is a border state sharing a long international boundary with Pakistan, a factor historically relevant to cross-border support for militancy and to drug trafficking routes.
static.socioEconomic: Analysts link the appeal of radical messaging to agrarian distress after the Green Revolution's plateauing returns, youth unemployment, migration pressures and the narcotics problem, alongside a sense of cultural and historical grievance.
static.whyInNews: The parole granted to a high-profile pro-Khalistan figure, accompanied by a 72-hour security deployment and a statewide alert, has refocused attention on Punjab's internal security management.
static.wayForward: A combination of intelligence-led policing, community engagement, monitoring of foreign funding under the FCRA, counter-radicalisation programmes, and addressing the underlying agrarian and employment distress that feeds grievance.
prelimsPointers: Punjab was reorganised on linguistic lines by the Punjab Reorganisation Act, 1966, which also created Haryana and the Union Territory of Chandigarh.
Punjab is a border state sharing an international boundary with Pakistan.
The Anandpur Sahib Resolution was adopted in 1973 and later became a reference point in the Punjab autonomy debate.
static.mainsAngle: Analyse the changing character of radicalism in Punjab and evaluate whether the state's response should privilege hard security measures or a broader socio-economic and community-engagement strategy.

prelims: A three-hour parole was granted to Amritpal Singh, accompanied by a 72-hour security deployment and a statewide alert in Punjab.
Parole is a short, conditional and discretionary release; furlough is a periodical release generally treated as a right under state prison rules.
Detention under the National Security Act can extend up to 12 months, with any detention beyond three months requiring the opinion of an Advisory Board.
Prisons and prison administration, including parole rules, are State List subjects, so norms vary across states.
stories.mainsQuestion: The grant of parole to a high-profile detainee amid heavy security raises the question of how states balance individual liberty with public order. Examine this dilemma in the context of Punjab's internal security landscape and preventive detention law in India.

stories.headline: GRAP curbs choke Delhi-NCR construction, delay real estate projects
stories.summary: Delhi-NCR's winter air quality crisis has again triggered Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) restrictions, and the resulting curbs on construction and demolition work are stalling real estate projects across the region. Developers report halted sites, disrupted deployment of labour and slipping completion timelines, with cost overruns likely to be passed on to buyers. At the same time, commentary on the same crisis argues that episodic emergency curbs are no substitute for year-round, citizen-backed action on pollution sources. The episode captures a familiar trade-off: short-term public-health protection against the economic and livelihood costs borne by the construction sector.
stories.whyItMatters: It tests the balance between environmental regulation and economic activity — a recurring GS-III theme linking air-pollution governance, urban infrastructure and informal labour welfare.

perspectives.take: Frames the crisis as a governance and citizen-accountability failure, arguing for year-round action rather than seasonal emergency measures.
Reports the economic fallout — GRAP construction bans delaying real estate projects in Delhi-NCR, with cost and timeline implications for developers and buyers.
